Q: Merging two sorted skip lists into a third one can be done in O(n)? A:

(The sizes of the sorted input arrays are m and n.)
Worst-case, you need m + n - 1 comparisons to merge them. O(m+n).
Best-case, IF the ranges don't overlap at all, the simplest merge algorithm will perform either m comparisons or n comparisons. (m if the first list comes first; n if the second list comes first.) Making O(max?(m,n)).
Looking ahead can let it skip many unnecessary comparisons, but it risks adding wasted comparisons.
Looking ahead once, at the beginning, in the above example with no overlap, would "reduce" the best-case comparisons from max?(m,n) to min(m,n) + log2(m) - 1, or O(min(m,n).)
Looking ahead while merging could avoid many comparisons IF the result isn't tightly interleaved (it receives some long "runs" from either input array). Looking ahead is guesswork, so the better guessing algorithm will be heuristic and a little adaptive. When merging random data, looking ahead by 1 costs a wasted comparison about as often as it saves a comparison. But with non-random data, the net savings can be larger. If long runs exist, adaptively looking ahead by a larger distances could save a lot of comparisons. You could do way better than O(m+n), depending on your skill at making the guessing algorithm and its match to the distributions of the actual nonrandom data. You'll need an algorithm for the forward guess (twice as far ahead as last time?) and one for the fallback guesses after a wrong guess (half as far ahead as the last guess?).
Another way to describe this approach is: After picking a side, see how many more in a row you can take from that side without checking them all.

Q: Does querying multiple EF Core DbSets in a single LINQ call still result in a single SQL query that is executed on the database? A:

Yes, Entity Framework, core and previous, always executed/executes one LINQ statement as one SQL query. When multiple DbSet are addressed in one LINQ query, the query will be translated into one SQL statement.

There is one exception - using AsSplitQuery, which was added in EF core 5 to prevent Cartesian Explosion. But that instruction doesn't depend on having one or multiple DbSets in one LINQ statement. It just executes multiple queries whenever necessary.

Q: Unable to enter critical section A:

Nothing is wrong with the lifetime of the section here: it is initialised once, before the thread starts, and never copied. The failure is scheduling. The worker holds the section for 100 ms and calls EnterCriticalSection again a few instructions after LeaveCriticalSection, and Windows gives no guarantee about the order in which waiting threads acquire ownership [1]. On Windows the FreePascal routines operate on this same operating-system object [2].

A contending thread may spin breifly and then block. When the worker leaves the critical section, the waiter can become eligible to run (enters the "ready" state"), but it has not received ownership. The worker is already executing and reaches its next EnterCriticalSection almost immediately, so it can take the newly free section before the waiter runs, and immediate reacquisition can win repeatedly, which looks like starvation. Since Windows Server 2003 with Service Pack 1, waiters are explictly documented as not served first-come, first-served, whereus Windows XP woke them generally in queue order [3]. Why I speak generally if because I am not fully sure, this is my observation. This anti-convoy design in place since Windows Server 2003 SP1 permits barging without guaranteeing that the releasing thread wins; the fairness was removed because handoff produces lock convoys [4] [5].

There was a comment

Microsoft may well have changed the undefined behaviour of the critical sections since XP.

The code is not undefined merely because the ordering changed; the mistake is relying on an acquisition order the API does not guarantee. The code itself is legal. Every API call in the example is used exactly as documented. Don't blame the API change or call the code "undefined"; the mistake was building on behavior that was observed but never guaranteed ;-)

Sleep(0) gives up the remainder of the time slice while leaving the worker ready to run; it guarantees neither that the waiting thread is selected nor that it acquires the section first [6]. Sleep(1) makes the worker non-runnable until its timeout expires, which leaves the waiter a much larger opprotunity to run and enter; after the timeout the worker merely becomes ready again, so this is a scheduling workaround, not an ordering guarantee [6]. Initialising the section inside the thread grants no ownership rights; my understanding is that any difference observed there is timing.

The evident design problem in this example is sleeping for 100 ms while holding the lock; a lock should protect only the short operation on shared state, and one held nearly all the time is a strong warning sign. Keep the protected region short, or hand work over explictly: Microsoft's migration advice for code that depended on the old ordering is a pair of event objects with which each thread signals the other to proceed [3], and the existing answer points the same way.

As a concrete example, my own FastMM4-AVX memory manager, a fork of Pierre le Riche's original FastMM4, faces the same need to synchronize heavily contended shared state. Its locking paths are designed to keep protected operations short and do not depend on FIFO acquisition of a critical section; configuartion options also allow different synchronization strategies. I mention it as an example from code I maintain, not as a requirement for solving this particluar problem [7], to merely show that there are plenty of synchronization techniques around :-)

Sources

  1. Microsoft, EnterCriticalSection
  2. Free Pascal Programmer's Guide, the chapter on critical sections
  3. Microsoft, Critical Section Objects
  4. Joe Duffy, Anti-convoy locks in Windows Server 2003 SP1 and Windows Vista
  5. Raymond Chen, A high waiter count on a free critical section may indicate a lock convoy
  6. Microsoft, Sleep
  7. FastMM4-AVX options
